articles.title: AI Can Write Frontend Code — What Should Developers Still Know?
articles.excerpt: A few years ago, writing frontend code meant spending a lot of time typing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript yourself. Today, AI can generate a complete component in seconds. You can ask: "Create a responsive…
articles.body: A few years ago, writing frontend code meant spending a lot of time typing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript yourself. Today, AI can generate a complete component in seconds. You can ask: "Create a responsive navbar in React with a mobile menu." And you may get working code almost immediately. So this raises an important question: If AI can write frontend code, what does a frontend developer need to know? I don't think the answer is "nothing." In fact, I think understanding the fundamentals is becoming even more important. AI Can Write Code. But Code Is Not the Whole Job.
articles.author: Ganesh Deshmukh

articles.title: When The Bot Has Three Tools Available And Confidently Picks The Wrong One
articles.excerpt: Once a conversational system gets wired up to more than one external tool, database lookup, calendar booking, payment processing, a new failure category appears that has nothing to do with whether any…
articles.body: Once a conversational system gets wired up to more than one external tool, database lookup, calendar booking, payment processing, a new failure category appears that has nothing to do with whether any individual tool works correctly. The model has to first decide which tool a given request actually calls for, and that routing decision, often treated as trivial during development, turns out to be one of the more fragile parts of the entire system once real, slightly ambiguous user requests start arriving.

articles.title: IQueryable vs IEnumerable: The Line Between C# and SQL
articles.excerpt: IQueryable vs IEnumerable: The Line Between C# and SQL You're filtering a million records. With one interface, the database does the work. With the other, your application drowns in memory. Same LINQ…
articles.body: IQueryable vs IEnumerable: The Line Between C# and SQL You're filtering a million records. With one interface, the database does the work. With the other, your application drowns in memory. Same LINQ syntax. Wildly different execution. Let's demystify where C# ends and SQL begins. The Two Worlds IEnumerable < Product > inMemory = products . Where ( p => p . Price > 100 ); IQueryable < Product > inDatabase = dbContext . Products . Where ( p => p . Price > 100 ); Same Where . Same lambda. Completely different animals.
articles.author: Nick

articles.title: The LLM Is Not Your Ranker. Four Layers, and It Only Touches Two
articles.excerpt: The pitch usually goes: send the catalog and the user's history to a model, get back a ranked list, delete the recommender. It demos beautifully on 200 items and falls over the moment the catalog has…
articles.body: The pitch usually goes: send the catalog and the user's history to a model, get back a ranked list, delete the recommender. It demos beautifully on 200 items and falls over the moment the catalog has 400,000 and the response has 80 milliseconds to come back. The 2026 research doesn't support the replacement story either. RecoChain (arxiv 2604.25787) proposes unified generative retrieval and ranking, then evaluates it against classic top-k ranking metrics, because the measurement requirement doesn't go away. RRCM (arxiv 2605.07129) frames LLM recommendation as retrieval-and-reasoning, where the model decides when to pull more evidence and optimization still runs against the final ranking reward, not against the quality of the model's prose.
articles.author: yulyabrocoders

articles.excerpt: I recently finished building a personal finance PWA. I started it because I wanted something that looked and felt like a premium native app (using a Liquid Glass UI design system), but with the speed…
articles.body: I recently finished building a personal finance PWA. I started it because I wanted something that looked and felt like a premium native app (using a Liquid Glass UI design system), but with the speed of the web. It’s built with React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and Firebase. It has some cool features like a built-in AppLock (PIN/Biometrics) and a multi-currency real-time dashboard. The problem is, I work a demanding full-time job and realized I have absolutely zero time for marketing or user acquisition. Instead of letting it rot on my hard drive, I’ve decided to sell the full source code and IP rights to someone who actually wants to launch it and monetize it (it's perfectly set up to add a premium tier or wrap in Capacitor for the App Stores).

articles.title: Do We Really Need React for Every Website?
articles.excerpt: If you're a frontend developer today, it's easy to feel like every new website should be built with React. Need a landing page? React. Need a portfolio? React. Need a company website? React. Need a si…
articles.body: If you're a frontend developer today, it's easy to feel like every new website should be built with React. Need a landing page? React. Need a portfolio? React. Need a company website? React. Need a simple blog? React. But there is one question we don't always ask: Do we actually need React for every website? The short answer is no . React is a powerful tool, but like any tool, it makes more sense when it solves a problem you actually have. What Problem Does React Solve? React is useful when the UI becomes interactive and complex. For example, imagine an application with: Product filters Shopping cart User authentication Notifications Modals Tabs Search Real-time updates Complex forms Shared application state Managing all of this with manual DOM manipulation can become difficult.

articles.body: From the beginning, Lanterns has used the town of Rushville to tell two connected mysteries set 10 years apart. articles.title: Lanterns Season 1, Episode 6 Review & Recap
articles.excerpt: Lanterns stumbles in Episode 6, as the series finally returns to the present day but struggles to maintain its narrative momentum. Read our full review.
articles.body: Warning: This review contains full spoilers for Lanterns Season 1, Episode 6! It was obvious from watching Lanterns Episode 5 that the series was due for a major shake-up in the remaining three installments. The 2016 storyline reached its fiery climax, as half of Rushville was destroyed, the Manhunter stood revealed, and John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) and Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) finally had their big falling-out. The series now pivots by returning fully to the 2026 timeline first teased in the pilot and digging into the mystery surrounding Hal's apparent murder. Lanterns is a very different show in Episode 6, and not necessarily for the better. Looking at Season 1 as a whole so far, the pacing is definitely a little strange.

Analemma over the Callanish Stones Explanation: If you went outside at the same time every day and took a picture that included the Sun , how would the Sun’s position change? articles.title: NASA Invites Media to Albania Artemis Accords Signing Ceremony
articles.excerpt: The Republic of Albania will sign the Artemis Accords during a ceremony at 12 p.m. EDT on Monday, Sept. 21, at NASA Headquarters in Washington, becoming the 73rd country signatory. NASA Deputy Adminis…
articles.body: Credit: NASA The Republic of Albania will sign the Artemis Accords during a ceremony at 12 p.m. EDT on Monday, Sept. 21, at NASA Headquarters in Washington, becoming the 73rd country signatory. NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson will host Albania’s Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Ferit Hoxha and Ambassador of the Republic of Albania to the United States Ervin Bushati for the ceremony, together with U.S. Department of State officials. This event is in person only. Media interested in attending must RSVP no later than 10 a.m. on Sept. 21 to: hq-media@mail.nasa.gov . NASA’s media accreditation policy is online.

articles.title: NASA-JAXA XRISM Mission Sees Pulsar Gathering Companion’s ‘Wind’
articles.excerpt: Using data from the Japan-led XRISM (X-ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission) observatory, astronomers have directly observed a giant star’s outflow, called a stellar wind, being captured by its compac…
articles.body: 5 min read NASA-JAXA XRISM Mission Sees Pulsar Gathering Companion’s ‘Wind’ Using data from the Japan-led XRISM (X-ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission) observatory, astronomers have directly observed a giant star’s outflow, called a stellar wind, being captured by its compact companion and providing the power source for strong X-ray flares. The research is part of NASA’s exploration of the extreme universe to better understand how the cosmos works. “We’ve never before seen clear indications of wind plasma falling onto a compact object,” said Roi Rahin, a researcher at UMBC (University of Maryland, Baltimore County) and NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.
